title: File character frequency
instructorPromptText: Write a C program that opens a file named `input.txt` for reading, counts the total occurrences of a specific character (e.g. 'e'), and prints the result. Handle file open failures.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the program verify that `fopen` successfully opened the file (i.e. did not return `NULL`) before attempting to read?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Attempting to read from a NULL file stream causes an immediate segmentation fault in C.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the program call `fclose` to release the file handle, even when file processing completes or errors occur?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Failing to close files causes file descriptor leaks. In long-running processes, this eventually exhausts available OS handles.

specGateDimensions.description: Is the variable storing the character read from the file declared as `int` rather than `char` to ensure `EOF` is detected correctly?
specGateDimensions.rationale: In C, `fgetc` returns an `int` so it can represent all valid char values plus `EOF` (-1). Using a `char` type can lead to early termination or infinite loops.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student reads from the file pointer without checking if it is NULL.
Student leaks file handles by not calling `fclose` before exiting.
Student stores the result of `fgetc` in a variable of type `char`, risking failure to detect EOF properly.
Student counts case-insensitively (e.g. counting both 'e' and 'E') when the spec only specifies character 'e'.
Student uses `fgets` or `fscanf` to read file contents in chunks rather than using `fgetc` char-by-char.
